hook.text: English is spoken in over 60 countries. That's not because it's the best language — it's because of empire.

buildup.text: Linguistic imperialism is the dominance of one language over others through colonialism, economics, and education.

discovery.text: Colonial powers forced their languages on subjects. English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese replaced local tongues.

twist.text: Today, English dominance continues through business, tech, and academia — even without direct colonial control.

climax.text: Linguistic imperialism doesn't just spread words. It spreads worldviews, marginalizing alternative ways of thinking.

punchline.text: A dominant language carries a dominant worldview.

quiz.question: What is linguistic imperialism?
options: One language dominating others through power and institutions
A natural process of language evolution

details.summary: Linguistic imperialism describes how dominant languages — particularly English — spread through colonial and postcolonial power structures, displacing indigenous languages. English's global dominance reflects political and economic power, not inherent linguistic superiority.
details.whyItMatters: The global spread of English is not neutral — it advantages native speakers economically and culturally while marginalizing others. Understanding linguistic imperialism reveals how language perpetuates global inequality.
takeaways: Dominant languages spread through political and economic power
English's global position reflects colonial history, not linguistic merit
Linguistic imperialism marginalizes speakers of other languages

faq.question: Is English spreading because it is a better language?
faq.answer: No. English spreads because of British colonial history and American economic and cultural dominance. Any language in that political position would have spread similarly. Linguistically, English is no more suited to international communication than any other language.

faq.question: How does linguistic imperialism affect education?
faq.answer: In many postcolonial nations, education is conducted in the former colonial language rather than local languages. Students must learn in a language they may not speak at home, creating educational disadvantage. This perpetuates the dominance of colonial languages across generations.
